title: The Gang Gives Frank an Intervention

jokes.text: Frank tries to drink wine inconspicuously from a can but his entire mouth is stained red
jokes.setup: Frank insists he's being inconspicuous by drinking wine from a soda can
jokes.punchline: His entire mouth is stained red, completely defeating the purpose
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank self-delusion — the gap between his perception and reality is the engine of his character. The visual of a stained red mouth paired with the word 'inconspicuous' is a tight, well-earned joke that sets the tone for the whole episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: i don't understand why you don't just use a cup.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: i'm trying to be inconspicuous.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: inconspicuous? your entire mouth is stained red, frank.

jokes.text: Frank is wearing a shirt inside out covered in what he claims is 'sap' because he got wasted and climbed a tree
jokes.setup: The gang notes Frank is covered in grease and his shirt is inside out
jokes.punchline: Frank clarifies it's sap, because he got wasted and climbed a tree
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'sap' vs 'grease' as the correction makes it funnier — Frank isn't embarrassed, he's clarifying the record. The drunk tree-climbing is a perfect Frank detail: depraved but somehow also childlike.

dialogue.line: you're wearing a shirt that's on inside out, and it's covered in grease.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: it's not grease; it's sap.

jokes.text: The gang arrives at what Frank said was a barbecue and it turns out to be a cemetery funeral
jokes.setup: Frank told the gang they were going to a barbecue
jokes.punchline: They're at a cemetery — specifically, at Frank's Uncle Max's funeral
jokes.explanation: A solid misdirect. The gang's disoriented reaction ('Who has a party in a cemetery?') followed by Frank's matter-of-fact 'Your Uncle Max' is efficiently structured. The bathos of the reveal — it's a funeral, not a barbecue — is classic Sunny.

dialogue.line: sap? how did you get covered in sap?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: i got really wasted. i must have climbed a tree.

jokes.text: Frank raises a toast at his uncle's funeral: 'Flush that turd down the drain!'
jokes.setup: They're at a formal funeral with bagpipes playing 'Amazing Grace'
jokes.punchline: Frank offers an enthusiastic and disrespectful toast about the deceased
jokes.explanation: Five words that do enormous comedic work. 'Flush that turd down the drain!' is perfectly Frank — crude, gleeful, and delivered at the exact wrong moment with zero self-awareness. The chuckle that follows seals it. Highly quotable, strong character specificity, economically ruthless.

dialogue.line: i feel like you've been standing on the edge of a cliff for a while now. i say hop off. let's see where you land.

jokes.text: The gang is completely underdressed at a funeral and Dee's primary concern is that it's 'embarrassing'
jokes.setup: They are at a funeral they didn't know they were attending
jokes.punchline: Dee says they're 'completely underdressed. It's embarrassing' — the embarrassment being about decorum, not grief
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat — Dee's self-consciousness over social embarrassment rather than genuine concern for the deceased is on-brand. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: i thought we were going to a barbecue, frank.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: it's more of a party in the park.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: we're at a cemetery.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: the party is in the cemetery.

jokes.text: Frank's stated reason for attending his uncle's funeral: 'I wanna bang your Aunt Donna'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks what Frank's angle is at the funeral
jokes.punchline: Frank wants to have sex with the newly widowed woman — the widow is Dennis's aunt
jokes.explanation: Frank's total lack of filter — the unashamed admission is funnier than any attempt at disguise. The timing, right after sincerely asking about the event, makes it land hard.

dialogue.line: who has a party in a cemetery?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: your uncle max. he just croaked. flush that turd down the drain!

jokes.text: 'I don't know how many years on this earth I got left. I'm gonna get real weird with it.'
jokes.setup: Dennis questions why Frank would want to bang their mom's sister at her husband's funeral
jokes.punchline: Frank's existential justification: limited time left, so maximum depravity
jokes.explanation: 'I'm gonna get real weird with it' is one of the most quotable Frank lines in the series. The delivery of mortality awareness pivoting immediately to sexual depravity is perfectly Frank. The economy is extraordinary — it encapsulates his entire Season 5 character arc in one sentence. High rewatch value because it functions as an accidental mission statement.

dialogue.line: what are we doing here, frank? what's your angle?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: i want to bang your aunt donna.

jokes.text: Frank lights a joint at a funeral, asking the gang to 'block the wind' while he 'roasts this bone'
jokes.setup: They're standing at a formal funeral service with bagpipes
jokes.punchline: Frank casually asks them to shield him so he can smoke a joint, using the term 'roast this bone' at a literal burial
jokes.explanation: The accidental dark wordplay of 'roast this bone' at a funeral gives this a little extra charge. It's a good escalation of Frank's funeral misbehavior.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: i don't know how many years on this earth i got left. i'm gonna get real weird with it.

jokes.text: The gang describes how they dealt with Gail the Snail as children: throwing her in a dryer, throwing salt on her
jokes.setup: Dee and Dennis explain that Gail 'glob[bed] onto' them at family parties and they couldn't get rid of her
jokes.punchline: The 'only way' to handle her was torture: dryer, salt — because she was 'the snail'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Sunny writing — the gang casually describes what is objectively child abuse while completely reframing it as a reasonable pest-control solution. The 'she made us do those things' justification is brilliant character work. The dryer-then-salt escalation is perfectly structured. This becomes the comedic backbone of the episode's third act.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: meanwhile, block the wind. i'm gonna roast this bone.

jokes.text: 'There's no joy in salting someone. Everyone loses.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee have just described torturing their cousin with salt and a dryer
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a somber, philosophical reflection on the act of salting a human being
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The gravity Dennis brings to 'there's no joy in salting someone, everyone loses' — as if he's reflecting on the futility of war — applied to salting a human cousin as a pest-control measure is an extraordinary piece of dark comedy economy. It's the perfect deadpan understatement that only Dennis Reynolds could deliver with this level of hollow gravitas. Highly quotable and completely recontextualizes what came before.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: gail the snail is the garbage pail cousin.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: oh, charlie, she is the worst.

jokes.text: Gail the Snail arrives: 'I'm a woman now. I'm not a virgin anymore.'
jokes.setup: The gang has just finished describing years of torturing Gail; she appears and they note she 'looks different'
jokes.punchline: Gail explains her transformation by announcing she is no longer a virgin, unsolicited
jokes.explanation: Perfect character introduction for Gail — she's socially oblivious, oversharing, and proudly announcing something nobody asked about at her father's funeral. 'Cool. Thank you. Okay.' from one of the gang is a great deflating reaction beat.

dialogue.line: the only way to get rid of her was to torch her, and that's what we did. yeah, we'd throw her in the dryer; we'd throw salt on her.

jokes.text: Gail's reaction to 'we're at your dad's funeral': 'What evs. I'm over it.'
jokes.setup: The gang reminds Gail she's at her father's funeral when she invites them to get high in her car
jokes.punchline: 'What evs. I'm over it.' — combined with the distinctive slurping sound
jokes.explanation: Gail's total indifference to her father's death, combined with the slurping affectation, establishes her as a monster in a completely different register than the main gang. 'What evs' at a funeral is a solid dark comedy beat.

dialogue.line: you throw salt on a snail and... it's supposed to shrivel up.

jokes.text: Gail's slurping sound introduced as a recurring character tic
jokes.setup: Gail is established as a uniquely repulsive character
jokes.punchline: She makes a loud, wet slurping sound that is inexplicably part of her personality
jokes.explanation: The slurping is a brilliantly simple physical comedy choice — it's disgusting, unexplained, and persistent. It's entirely conveyed through the transcript's notation '[Slurps]' and the gang's reactions. High character integration because it only works for this specific character. Sets up a running gag.

dialogue.line: what kind of person salts another human being? it's terrible. there's no joy in salting someone; everyone loses.

jokes.text: The gang scrambles to get rid of Gail using any excuse, agreeing to anything to get her away: 'Five minutes. Anything. Yes. Anything. Whatever you say.'
jokes.setup: Gail invites the gang to her car for medical marijuana and lingers
jokes.punchline: The whole gang falls over each other making empty promises just to get her to walk away
jokes.explanation: The ensemble desperation is well-played. The rhythm of overlapping reassurances is a good comedic texture, showing the gang's collective cowardice around Gail.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: i'm not a virgin anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: cool. thank you.

jokes.text: 'See, this is what happens when you don't have salt.' / 'My God. There's not enough salt in the world for her.'
jokes.setup: Gail has just departed after being excessively clingy
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately frames her departure as evidence that they need salt — referring to their earlier torture method
jokes.explanation: Quick, sharp callback that earns a second laugh on the established salting mythology. 'There's not enough salt in the world for her' is a genuinely good line — hyperbolic and logical within the episode's internal rules.

dialogue.line: we're at your dad's funeral, gail.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: whatevs. i'm over it.

jokes.text: Frank left Donna multiple voicemails 'congratulating her on her husband's death.' He explains: 'Well, I was pretty baked.'
jokes.setup: Donna expresses surprise at Frank's presence
jokes.punchline: Frank already sent congratulatory voicemails about the death; his defense is simply that he was high
jokes.explanation: Congratulating someone on their spouse's death via voicemail is delightfully specific and depraved. 'I was pretty baked' as the entire explanation is pitch-perfect Frank economy.

dialogue.line: see? that's what happens when you don't have salt. my god, there's not enough salt in the world for her.

jokes.text: Frank's pickup line to the widow: 'What better way to get back at them in the grave, really stick it to 'em, if you and me plowed?'
jokes.setup: Frank proposes they sleep together as revenge on their respective deceased/ex spouses
jokes.punchline: The word 'plowed' used as the culmination of this romantic proposition, followed by his grinding teeth and 'Hmm?'
jokes.explanation: The seduction logic is perfectly Frank: appeal to shared resentment of dead people as foreplay. 'Plowed' is the ideal word choice — crude and blunt. The teeth-grinding pause after is a great visual beat implying he thinks this is suave.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: i have a proposition for you. i think you and me ought to bang.

jokes.text: Mac approaches Donna and sighs: 'Barbara's ex-lover' — implying he had an affair with Frank's deceased wife
jokes.setup: Mac introduces himself to Donna at the funeral in a way that suggests he's about to say something ordinary
jokes.punchline: He identifies himself as the ex-lover of Frank's dead wife — a revelation delivered with inexplicable pride
jokes.explanation: The reveal is planted early and paid off later (joke #40). The setup here — the sigh, the pause, the proud identification — is excellent economy. Donna's stunned silence is the punchline. Great slow-burn setup.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: max never liked me; i hated him. barbara didn't like you. you despised her! now what better way to get back at them in the grave-- really stick it to 'em-- if you and me plowed?

jokes.text: Mac introduces himself to Donna as Barbara's 'ex-lover' — reaction beat as Donna clearly goes silent
jokes.setup: Mac approaches Donna at the funeral and introduces himself
jokes.punchline: He identifies himself as Barbara's 'ex-lover' (Frank's dead wife) — a bomb drop that leaves Donna speechless, indicated by her not saying anything
jokes.explanation: Mac casually identifying as the dead wife's ex-lover at a family funeral is a good cringe moment. The reaction beat — Donna goes silent, Mac clarifies 'I was just breathing' — is funny and awkward. Plants the Barbara revelation that pays off later.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: hey, i'm mac. barbara's ex-lover? she may have mentioned. you were gonna say something?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: no.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: you said...

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: no?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: no, i was just breathing.

jokes.text: The gang explains Frank's main problem to the therapist: 'He is trying to bang our aunt. That's the big one.'
jokes.setup: The intervention therapist asks what Frank is struggling with most
jokes.punchline: The gang identifies not substance abuse but the aunt-banging as the primary concern
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the therapist-client dynamic. The therapist's dry correction ('these things deal more with drug and alcohol abuse') is funny precisely because the gang immediately co-opts it back into the aunt problem.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: but if i'm being honest, my problem's less with the fact that he's drinking more that he's doing it without me. and then i start thinking, 'what's wrong with me? am i not fun to drink with?'

jokes.text: Charlie admits his problem with Frank's drinking is less that he's drinking and more that he's doing it without Charlie, making Charlie feel unwanted
jokes.setup: The therapist asks how Frank's drinking has affected them
jokes.punchline: Charlie's grievance isn't about Frank's wellbeing — it's about FOMO and feeling left out of drinking sessions
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie — his emotional vulnerability is completely misdirected. He's not concerned about Frank's health; he's hurt that Frank drinks without him. This reframes the entire intervention premise in the most Charlie way possible. The therapist's sincere reassurance makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: well, frank's usually carrying, like, a little gun around with him and he doesn't really hesitate to use it.

jokes.text: Therapist reassures Charlie: 'You're plenty of fun to drink with. You get really, really drunk and then you get reckless.'
jokes.setup: Charlie worries he's not fun to drink with
jokes.punchline: The therapist — who is supposed to be a professional — sincerely reassures him by confirming his recklessness is an asset
jokes.explanation: The therapist is already being corrupted by this group. Describing 'getting really drunk and reckless' as a positive drinking quality is a great ironic inversion of her professional role.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: if we maybe ambush frank with a net or some kind of, like, rope device, the gun will maybe drop out of his waist belt.

jokes.text: Dennis suggests the intervention should involve 'ambushing' Frank and 'berating him into becoming the guy we wanna be around'
jokes.setup: The therapist explains the proper approach to interventions
jokes.punchline: Dennis describes the goal not as helping Frank but as making Frank convenient for the gang
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-serving reframe of an intervention as a tool to modify Frank's behavior for the gang's comfort is sharp character writing. The therapist's 'you certainly don't berate him' is a good straight-man beat.

dialogue.speaker: Therapist
dialogue.line: you're drinking wine out of a soda can.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Therapist
dialogue.line: oh, you put wine in the soda can you didn't know, did you?

jokes.text: Mac suggests they should be armed at the intervention because Frank carries a gun and 'doesn't really hesitate to use it'
jokes.setup: Mac suggests coming at Frank 'with an iron fist'
jokes.punchline: The intervention requires weapons because Frank is armed and dangerous; they advise the therapist to put a gun in her pants
jokes.explanation: The progression from 'intervention' to 'everyone bring guns' to 'she can put it in her pants' is a great escalation. The therapist's growing alarm is the perfect straight-man reaction. The gang normalizing firearms at a support group is quintessential Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: stole frank's idea. yeah, yeah, yeah. it actually is a pretty good one. i mean, the guy's got great ideas. he's a smart man.

jokes.text: Charlie proposes ambushing Frank with a net or rope device so his gun falls out of his waistband
jokes.setup: The gang is debating how to safely disarm Frank at the intervention
jokes.punchline: Charlie's tactical solution is a net — 'some kind of rope device' — to disarm him
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'rope device' characterization and the therapist's 'you wanna bring him in in a net?' is a good absurdist beat. Part of the larger gun-at-intervention escalation sequence.

dialogue.line: but i do feel like she just tried an intervention on us. did you intervene on us? is that what that was?

jokes.text: The therapist calls out that they're drinking wine out of a soda can during the intervention planning meeting
jokes.setup: The therapist notes the incongruity of their intervention advice given their own behavior
jokes.punchline: She's talking about bringing guns to an intervention, and they're drinking wine out of soda cans — the callback to the opening gag
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the gang has adopted Frank's canned wine habit while simultaneously trying to stage an intervention on him. The irony is well-structured and the therapist's exasperation sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: i feel like you've lost control of the room here and really we're the ones that are running things now.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'You stole Frank's idea.' / Gang admits the canned wine is actually genius
jokes.setup: The therapist has just pointed out they're drinking wine from soda cans
jokes.punchline: The gang pivots to defending and praising Frank's canned wine innovation — the very behavior they're trying to intervene on
jokes.explanation: The gang inadvertently defending the subject of their intervention's lifestyle choices while in the act of planning the intervention is a solid ironic reversal. Dennis's 'the guy's got great ideas, he's a smart man' is good.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: where did you come from?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: i've been walking next to you the entire time.

jokes.text: Dennis turns on the therapist: 'I feel like you've lost control of the room here. And we're the ones running things now.'
jokes.setup: The therapist tries to redirect the meeting
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses her professional authority and declares the gang is now in charge
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis narcissism — he seizes power in a situation where he has no authority, and the gang follows him like it's a coup. His 'I've lost my trust in you' about the therapist is very Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: i think you should bang gail the snail.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: my niece?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: gail the snail?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: yeah, dude. what's more depraved than that, huh?

jokes.text: The gang dismisses the therapist and grabs her pamphlets on the way out; Dennis says 'don't beat her while she's down'
jokes.setup: They've just fired the therapist and are ushering her out
jokes.punchline: After being dismissive and rude, Dennis ironically cautions against 'beating her while she's down' — the hypocrisy is the joke
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. The gang's total lack of self-awareness about their own cruelty is on-brand. The pamphlet-grabbing is a nice visual detail reinforcing Charlie's illiteracy setup.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: what's in it for you? jesus. what's in it for you?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: don't worry about what's in it for me, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: my god, you are disgusting. a disgusting animal.

jokes.text: "She didn't do that great of a job." / "No, but don't beat her while she's down."
jokes.setup: The gang has just fired the therapist and is showing her out
jokes.punchline: Mac critiques the therapist's performance; Dee's response ('don't beat her while she's down') implies the therapist has been crushed — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Decent tag on the therapist-firing scene. 'Don't beat her while she's down' implies the therapist has already been destroyed, which is funny given they just hired her. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: when was the last time we played 'nightcrawlers' together, frank?

jokes.text: Frank is walking down the street gurgling/belching with Charlie barely visible next to him — Charlie says 'I've been walking next to you the entire time'
jokes.setup: Frank is extremely drunk, belching and gurgling, and suddenly startles when Charlie speaks
jokes.punchline: Charlie has been right next to him the whole time; Frank was too wasted to notice
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy implied by the transcript — Frank so drunk he doesn't perceive the person next to him. The 'Oh! Where'd you come from?' is a solid reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: what is that?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: well... it's not about you.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: why don't you just write it down?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: yeah, but you said it. you said 'nightcrawlers,' and now i feel like i can't move past it.

jokes.text: Charlie's suggestion: Frank should bang Gail the Snail because 'what's more depraved than that?' and 'you're not blood related, so it's not that weird'
jokes.setup: Frank has been obsessing about how to bang Donna for the last five miles (of walking)
jokes.punchline: Charlie's alternative: bang the niece — framed as a helpful, logical suggestion with the reassurance that it's 'not that weird'
jokes.explanation: Charlie's moral calculus — 'not blood related so it's not that weird' as a positive endorsement of sleeping with your uncle's niece — is a great dark absurdist beat. His enthusiasm and Frank's belching acceptance is perfectly disgusting comedy teamwork.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: what it sounds like is that you two crawl around like worms in the night. that's what it sounds like.

jokes.text: Frank belches enormously and repeatedly while Charlie asks 'what's in it for you?' — Frank's belching prevents any answer
jokes.setup: Charlie grows suspicious of Charlie's motives for pushing Gail
jokes.punchline: Frank's reply is entirely consumed by enormous belches; Charlie's reaction ('You are disgusting. A disgusting animal.') is the button
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy from Frank's belching is a low-craft but effective gross-out bit. Charlie's escalating disgust sells it. The belching as evasion is a clever structural choice even if the execution is crude.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: i am loving this canned wine thing. i think it's brilliant. right? i mean, i'm active, i'm gesturing with my hands, and i don't feel restricted.

jokes.text: Dee realizes she'll have to dictate her intervention letter to Charlie because he can't read or write
jokes.setup: Dee and Charlie try to write letters for the intervention
jokes.punchline: The assumption is simply stated — Charlie can't read or write, so Dee must dictate; Charlie accepts this as normal
jokes.explanation: Charlie's illiteracy being treated as a mundane logistical fact is a good running character detail. The matter-of-fact way Dee states it and Charlie accepts it is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: i'm starting to think we need to intervene on you for your goddamn illiteracy.

jokes.text: Charlie's intervention letter opens with the question: 'When was the last time we played Night Crawlers together, Frank?'
jokes.setup: Charlie is dictating a heartfelt letter to Frank about their friendship
jokes.punchline: His deepest concern is the cessation of an activity called 'Night Crawlers'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Night Crawlers' is introduced as a mysterious concept and immediately becomes the comedic obsession of multiple characters. It's the perfect Charlie obscurity — something deeply personal and inexplicable that he treats with complete sincerity. Dee's immediate demand to know what it is mirrors the audience. The joke is the question itself — deeply absurd, perfectly Charlie, and structurally brilliant because it derails the entire scene.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: we did a bunch of those monster energy drinks and dry-humped. it was awful. i think she gave me poison ivy.

jokes.text: Dee cannot move past the phrase 'Night Crawlers' and demands an explanation; Charlie insists 'it's not about you'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to continue dictating his letter; Dee is fixated on 'Night Crawlers'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's attempts to maintain privacy while Dee escalates her need to know; Dee correctly guesses it involves crawling like worms at night
jokes.explanation: Dee's guess — 'What it sounds like is that you two crawl around like worms in the night' — and Charlie's non-denial is comic gold. Her frustration, Charlie's secretive defensiveness, and the increasingly obvious nature of what Night Crawlers must be create a perfect slow-burn joke.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: kick, yes. kick in, no. that door is solid, which is the good news. the bad news is the window is not.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis burst in banging pots and pans, yelling 'We got you! Intervention!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have apparently been planning an ambush element to the intervention
jokes.punchline: They burst in with noise-making implements to 'disorient' Frank — but Frank isn't even there
jokes.explanation: Good physical energy. The impracticality of the plan (the pain from banging pots is 'a little agitating') is a nice self-undermining detail. The group's enthusiasm for tactics over substance is classic Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: i'm giving frank a handy under the table. that is true.

jokes.text: Dennis delivers a monologue on why canned wine is superior: 'I'm active. I'm gesturing with my hands. If I was holding a wine glass, I'd be spilling everywhere.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of intervention planning, Dennis pivots to praising canned wine
jokes.punchline: His lengthy, passionate defense of canned wine is completely irrelevant to the intervention; the gang debates wine mobility instead of helping Frank
jokes.explanation: Dennis's wine mobility lecture while supposedly planning an intervention is perfect character work — his elaborate justifications for trivial things. Part of the running canned wine gag that beautifully mirrors the episode's theme of the gang being their own problem.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: look, snail, back off because you're just mashing it now.

jokes.text: 'We're not intervening on Frank for a lack of good ideas.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been praising Frank's canned wine idea during the intervention planning
jokes.punchline: Mac's dry clarification that Frank's flaw is not creativity
jokes.explanation: Very economical line that cuts through the nonsense beautifully. It's the most sensible thing said in the scene, which is ironic coming from Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: you're 33 years old. you're supposed to be sexually active. you're not supposed to be fondling your uncle under a table.

jokes.text: The pamphlets Charlie grabbed from the therapist's office have nothing to do with intervention; Dennis threatens to 'intervene on [Charlie] for his goddamn illiteracy'
jokes.setup: Charlie suggests consulting the pamphlets he grabbed
jokes.punchline: None of the pamphlets are about intervention — Charlie can't read — and Dennis pivots to threatening a second intervention for Charlie's illiteracy
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — the intervention now has a second target (Charlie). The illiteracy joke pays off on the earlier setup. 'You are getting real dumb' from Dee is a solid pile-on.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: we told him there was a giant grease fire and he had to come down immediately.

jokes.text: Charlie asks: 'What does that word [illiteracy] even mean?' while storming off to get the therapist back
jokes.setup: Dennis accuses Charlie of illiteracy
jokes.punchline: Charlie doesn't know what 'illiteracy' means — the perfect self-own that proves the accusation
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest jokes in the episode. Charlie asking what 'illiteracy' means in the moment of being accused of illiteracy is a perfect self-defeating loop. The delivery must be indignant. Only Charlie can make this joke land — it requires total sincerity. Extremely quotable and perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: where's the goddamn fire?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: intervention! you're surrounded, frank. there's nowhere for you to go. you're trapped.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he pushed Frank toward Gail specifically to 'swoop in on Donna' himself
jokes.setup: Frank is at Gail's house; Mac appears unexpectedly
jokes.punchline: Mac's entire Gail suggestion was a Machiavellian scheme to clear the field for Donna — 'That's right, bitch'
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the Charlie scene from earlier. Mac calling Frank 'bitch' while triumphantly explaining his scheme is very Mac. The logic of the scheme is delightfully petty.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: a roast? i've always wanted to be roasted. oh, wait, let me just switch gears here. fire up this spliff.

jokes.text: Gail and Frank's night together: 'We did a bunch of Monster Energy drinks and dry humped. It was awful. I think she gave me poison ivy.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks if Gail and Frank 'banged'
jokes.punchline: Their depressing encounter involved Monster Energy drinks, dry humping, and apparent poison ivy — nobody is happy
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The specific combination of Monster Energy drinks + dry humping + poison ivy is a perfect trifecta of degradation. Each element is funnier than the last. The escalation from 'we did a bunch of Monster Energy drinks' (a weird non-sexual detail as preamble) to 'dry humped' (more depressing than explicit) to 'it was awful / I think she gave me poison ivy' (both characters are victims) is brilliantly structured. Extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: she ain't funny. next.

jokes.text: Gail has broken into Frank's apartment by going through the window after failing to kick down the door
jokes.setup: Frank wakes up to find Gail in his apartment making breakfast
jokes.punchline: She explains: 'Kick, yes. Kick in, no. That door is solid... the bad news is the window is not.'
jokes.explanation: Gail's break-in logic is delivered with the confidence of a home security consultant, which is a great character beat. 'That door is solid, which is the good news' as reassurance after breaking the window is an excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: it's a game where they crawl around in the night like worms.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: i never said that.

jokes.text: 'I haven't any idea, honestly. I'm giving Frank a handy under the table.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Gail's mother (Donna) has walked in; Frank asks what's going on
jokes.punchline: Gail cheerfully announces she is performing a sex act on Frank under the table in front of her mother
jokes.explanation: The delivery of 'I haven't any idea, honestly' as a confused preamble before the specific revelation is perfect comic structure. The cheerfulness, the specificity, the audience — her own mother — and Frank's confirming 'that is true' all compound the discomfort beautifully. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Uncle Max's Friend
dialogue.line: you banged my dead wife?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: well, she was alive at the time. did you not know that?

jokes.text: Frank: 'Look, Snail — Back off. Because you're just mashing it now. It's not...'
jokes.setup: Gail is performing the act under the table; Frank tries to diplomatically redirect her
jokes.punchline: Frank's complaint is not about the act itself but the technique — 'you're just mashing it now'
jokes.explanation: Frank's critique of Gail's technique rather than the act itself in front of her mother is a brilliant escalation. The fact that he calls her 'Snail' mid-complaint adds insult to injury.

dialogue.speaker: Gail
dialogue.line: salt the snail. you salt her. wait, wait. you guys want to go? no, no! wait. i have glow sticks. go, go!

jokes.text: Donna: 'You're 33 years old. You're supposed to be sexually active. You're not supposed to be fondling your uncle under a table.'
jokes.setup: Gail's defense: 'Mom, I'm sexually active now. Get over it.'
jokes.punchline: Donna's response distinguishes between acceptable adult behavior and specifically fondling uncles under tables
jokes.explanation: Donna's line is a masterclass in absurdist straight-man delivery. She validates sexual activity at 33 — a reasonable position — while adding the specific carve-out for 'fondling your uncle under a table.' The reasonableness of the first half makes the specificity of the second half devastating. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: nobody likes salting a snail, but she gives you no choice. she doesn't leave you with any options.

jokes.text: "We're not blood related. Will you just please leave her alone?" — Frank defending Gail to Donna
jokes.setup: Donna tells Gail to stop fondling Frank; Frank defends Gail
jokes.punchline: Frank's defense of the indefensible uses the 'not blood related' argument — the same logic Charlie used when suggesting this pairing
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the 'not blood related' justification introduced by Charlie is now Frank's actual defense. It's a funny echo, though it's not as strong as the original deployment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: well, we did all the work, didn't we?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: we did.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: so we can't really pay you 'cause of that.

jokes.text: Frank attempts to trade: 'I dump the Snail if you and I go out.' Dennis: 'I called her first at the funeral. Fair is fair.'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to negotiate with Donna using Gail as a bargaining chip
jokes.punchline: Dennis invokes 'dibs' logic — he 'called her first at the funeral' — as though Donna is an object to be claimed
jokes.explanation: Dennis's 'fair is fair' logic about calling dibs on a widow at her husband's funeral is very Dennis — his warped sense of property rights applied to people. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Gail declares Frank her boyfriend and says she's leaving with him; Frank: 'I am not your boyfriend.' Gail takes eggs anyway.
jokes.setup: Everyone is asked to leave; Gail refuses and says she's going with Frank
jokes.punchline: Frank explicitly denies the relationship; Gail ignores him entirely and takes his eggs
jokes.explanation: Gail's oblivious appropriation of Frank's relationship status and eggs is a good character beat, though by this point in the Gail sequence the novelty is slightly diminished.

jokes.text: The gang lured Frank to the intervention by telling him there was 'a giant grease fire'
jokes.setup: The therapist asks how they informed Frank about the intervention
jokes.punchline: They told him there was a giant grease fire — the most un-intervention-like lure imaginable, but perfectly suited to Frank
jokes.explanation: The grease fire lure is characteristically Sunny — the gang's solution to every problem involves the most chaotic possible approach. The therapist's visible dismay sells it.

jokes.text: The therapist's face upon learning the intervention is happening at a bar
jokes.setup: The gang assumes the therapist wouldn't have issues with their intervention setup
jokes.punchline: She clearly does — 'I'm assuming you wouldn't have lured him down with a fire. Is that what your face is doing right now?'
jokes.explanation: The therapist's face being so expressive that someone has to describe it is a solid bit. The 'I wouldn't have an intervention at a bar either' continuation shows her progressive resignation.

jokes.text: "All mistakes we've made on our own, so it's good that you're here."
jokes.setup: The therapist has listed multiple ways the gang has already botched the intervention
jokes.punchline: Dennis enthusiastically agrees that they've made all these mistakes independently — framed as a reason to be glad she's there, with no acknowledgment of how bad the mistakes are
jokes.explanation: Dennis's cheerful acknowledgment of their failures without any self-awareness is perfectly in character. 'All mistakes we've made on our own' as a boast is a good ironic line.

jokes.text: Frank enters the bar yelling 'Where's the goddamn fire?' with a cocked gun; the gang screams 'Intervention!' and surrounds him
jokes.setup: Frank has been told there's a grease fire; he arrives armed and ready
jokes.punchline: The intervention chaos: screaming, surrounding him, chanting 'you're trapped' — Frank has his gun out
jokes.explanation: The payoff of multiple setups — the gun, the fire lure, the ambush tactics — all converging simultaneously is well-structured farce. The chaos of everyone screaming 'intervention' is visually funny.

jokes.text: Frank hears 'we're gonna point out your faults' and immediately misunderstands it as a roast: 'A roast? I've always wanted to be roasted!'
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Frank they're going to 'get all in his face and point out his faults'
jokes.punchline: Frank interprets this as a Friars Club roast and is DELIGHTED — immediately lighting a joint
jokes.explanation: Frank reframing the intervention as a roast is a brilliant comedic pivot that makes the entire intervention structure collapse. His enthusiasm — 'I've always wanted to be roasted!' followed by lighting a joint — is perfect Frank. The intervention now has to work around Frank's delight at being insulted.

jokes.text: The therapist's attempt at sincerity: 'Everyone's here because they care about you and want you to get well.' Frank: 'She ain't funny. Next.'
jokes.setup: The therapist tries to deliver a sincere intervention message
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses her as a bad roast comedian — 'she ain't funny, next'
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'she ain't funny, next' applied to a therapist's sincere expression of concern is a devastating subversion. It perfectly captures how Frank's reframing renders all genuine help useless. Economically brilliant — three words destroy the intervention's purpose.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Frank, you're an asshole.' Frank: 'Ah! That's it. Now rain down on me. Come on.'
jokes.setup: The gang tries to shift to actual insults, hoping that works better
jokes.punchline: Frank loves it — the intervention is now his dream roast; he's actively encouraging more abuse
jokes.explanation: Frank's gleeful 'rain down on me' in response to being called an asshole is a great inversion — the gang's cruelty is now Frank's pleasure, completely neutralizing the intervention's power.

jokes.text: Night Crawlers reveal at the intervention: 'Why do we never play Night Crawlers anymore?' / Frank: 'What is Night Crawlers?' / Dee: 'It's a game where they crawl around in the night like worms.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's heartfelt intervention moment is the Night Crawlers question
jokes.punchline: Frank doesn't know what Night Crawlers is; Dee states flatly what it is — confirming her guess from earlier was correct
jokes.explanation: The Night Crawlers payoff is the comedic peak of the episode. The triple-beat structure is perfect: Charlie's sincere grievance, Frank's confusion (suggesting he doesn't even remember the thing Charlie treasures), and Dee's flat confirmation that it is literally what it sounds like — grown men crawling around like worms at night. Charlie's 'is nothing private, Frank?' and then immediately confirming he wants to continue playing is extraordinary character comedy. Frank's 'I like that game, I don't wanna stop playing it' caps it perfectly. This is what this show does better than almost anything else.

jokes.text: Frank promises to resume Night Crawlers; Charlie celebrates ecstatically: 'Whoo! Ahh! Yeah!' — the intervention has succeeded for Charlie
jokes.setup: Charlie's intervention goal was Night Crawlers; Frank agrees to resume
jokes.punchline: Charlie's elated celebration — the intervention, designed for Frank's benefit, has actually served Charlie's goal of crawling around like worms
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Charlie's entire arc: the intervention works perfectly — but only for restoring Night Crawlers. His 'Whoo!' celebration in the middle of an intervention for someone else's alcoholism is a perfect absurdist button.

jokes.text: Gail appears at the intervention and Mac is revealed to be 'with' her — 'Me and Mac are together'
jokes.setup: The intervention is in chaos; Gail suddenly appears with Mac
jokes.punchline: Mac is apparently dating Gail the Snail now — the gang immediately calls for an intervention on Mac
jokes.explanation: Gail's appearance mid-intervention with Mac is a good escalation twist. The gang immediately redirecting 'Intervention!' at Mac is a great running gag deployment. Mac insisting 'she followed me home' is a perfect deflection.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he was going to Donna's house 'to bang her because she reminds me so much of your mom, which is the best sex I ever had'
jokes.setup: Frank asks what Mac is doing with Donna
jokes.punchline: Mac admits he wanted to sleep with Donna because she resembles Barbara (Frank's dead wife, Dennis's mother) — the best sex of his life
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Mac/Barbara setup from the funeral. The specific detail that Barbara is 'the best sex [Mac] ever had' — said directly to Frank and Dennis — is a devastating revelation. Frank's 'You banged my dead wife?' / Mac's 'Well, she was alive at the time' exchange is a perfect comedy beat. Mac adding 'Did you not know that?' as if it was public knowledge is extraordinary. This is a major escalation that ripples through the room.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Well, she was alive at the time. But- Did you not know that?' — delivered as genuine clarification
jokes.setup: Frank: 'You banged my dead wife?'
jokes.punchline: Mac clarifies she was alive at the time — the most obvious possible clarification — then adds 'Did you not know that?' as if Frank should have been aware of the affair
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and among the strongest individual beats in the series. The structure is flawless: 'You banged my dead wife?' → 'She was alive at the time' (factual correction that completely misses the point) → 'Did you not know that?' (implying the affair was common knowledge and Frank is simply uninformed). Mac's total obliviousness to why this is devastating — treating it as a factual misunderstanding rather than a betrayal — is extraordinary character writing. Extremely quotable. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: Frank tries to wave it off: 'It's cool, man. It's cool.' — then immediately calls for an intervention on Mac
jokes.setup: Frank has just learned Mac slept with his late wife
jokes.punchline: Frank dismisses it with 'it's cool' but then pivots to 'intervention, intervention' — using the episode's vocabulary to call for Mac's punishment
jokes.explanation: Frank's immediate 'it's cool' followed by calling for an intervention demonstrates the episode's running gag perfectly — 'intervention' has become a reflexive social weapon rather than a therapeutic tool.

jokes.text: Dennis covers for Mac: 'Look, he's got a weird fetish for older women, so don't hold it against him. I don't have an older-woman fetish.'
jokes.setup: Mac just admitted to sleeping with Frank's wife and wanting to sleep with Donna because she resembles her
jokes.punchline: Dennis pathologizes it as an older-woman fetish; Mac immediately denies this specific diagnosis while not denying the behavior
jokes.explanation: Mac's specific objection to 'fetish' while having just admitted to exactly what constitutes a fetish for older women is a good irony beat. Dennis's breezy minimization of a serious betrayal is very Dennis.

jokes.text: The word 'Intervention!' has become a meaningless chant being applied to everyone in the room
jokes.setup: The intervention was for Frank but has expanded to include Mac and Gail
jokes.punchline: The word 'Intervention' is now being shouted as a general-purpose crowd-control word with no specific target, losing all meaning
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — the word has been repeated so many times and applied to so many people that it's now meaningless noise. Dennis's meta-comment ('there's a lot of them being thrown around, I'm having trouble keeping track') is a good self-aware joke.

jokes.text: The gang loses track of which interventions are active: 'Let's cool it with the intervention stuff for a second, 'cause there's a lot of 'em being thrown around and I'm having a little trouble keeping track'
jokes.setup: Multiple simultaneous 'interventions' have been called (Frank, Charlie, Mac, Gail)
jokes.punchline: Mac requests a pause on interventions due to volume; the word has become meaningless through overuse
jokes.explanation: Meta acknowledgment of the episode's running gag. Mac being the one to call for order is funny given his role in causing the chaos. The word 'intervention' losing all meaning through overuse mirrors the episode's theme.

jokes.text: The gang decides the most important intervention is on Gail to get her out of their lives
jokes.setup: Mac tries to prioritize the many concurrent interventions
jokes.punchline: The 'most important' intervention is not for Frank's alcoholism but to remove Gail from their social circle
jokes.explanation: Good illustration of the gang's self-serving nature — the intervention was never really about Frank. Functional but not a standout.

jokes.text: Gail invites everyone to 'do shots and get crazy' mid-intervention; the gang stonewalls her
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to stage Gail's intervention
jokes.punchline: Gail completely fails to register the hostility and suggests shots instead
jokes.explanation: Gail's obliviousness is consistent character work but this instance is less surprising than her earlier appearances.

jokes.text: Frank produces salt and they begin chasing Gail around the bar throwing salt on her; everyone screaming 'Salt the Snail!' / 'Ya, ya, ya!'
jokes.setup: Gail won't leave; Dennis established that salt is the only way to handle her
jokes.punchline: The whole gang chases Gail with salt shakers while she runs — the entire bar participates in this ritual
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the entire salting mythology. The escalation from childhood torture to adult bar chase is brilliantly earned. 'He's got the salt!' and the collective 'Salt the Snail!' chant is a magnificent setpiece. Gail then trying to invite them to a rave with glow sticks while being chased with salt is an inspired detail. This is the visual comedy centerpiece of the episode.

jokes.text: Gail, mid-salt-attack: 'I was gonna invite you guys to a rave, but now I don't wanna hang out with you anymore.' / 'I have glow sticks.'
jokes.setup: The gang is chasing Gail with salt shakers
jokes.punchline: Gail's objection is not the salt but the social slight — she's hurt they're not accepting her rave invitation; she deploys glow sticks as a lure
jokes.explanation: Gail's completely misdirected hurt feelings — not about the salt, but about the rave rejection — is perfect character work. 'I have glow sticks' as a last-ditch bribe while fleeing people throwing salt at her is an extraordinary detail. This is the best Gail moment.

jokes.text: Post-salting guilt: 'Nobody likes salting the Snail, but she gives you no choice.' / 'She doesn't leave you with any options.'
jokes.setup: The gang has just driven Gail out with salt; they're now processing the experience
jokes.punchline: They repeat the same post-salting rationalizations from the opening scene verbatim — 'nobody likes it,' 'no choice,' 'no options' — perfectly mirroring the earlier guilt
jokes.explanation: The post-salting guilt mirroring the earlier guilt conversation is a great structural callback — the gang has done the exact same thing they described with the same rationalizations, proving they've learned nothing and can't stop themselves. 'What a horrible thing' said by people who just did it again is perfect irony. Well-structured and earned.

jokes.text: Aftermath of salting: 'That was a terrible experience for me.' / 'Nobody likes salting the Snail, but she gives you no choice.'
jokes.setup: The salt chase is over; Gail is gone
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers another solemn reflection on the regrettable necessity of salting — identical to his earlier 'no joy in salting' line
jokes.explanation: Second deployment of the 'nobody enjoys salting' philosophy. Slightly less fresh than the original, but 'she doesn't leave you with any options' is a good addition to the salting mythology.

jokes.text: The canned wine discussion breaks out post-salting; the gang evangelizes canned wine to Frank and the therapist
jokes.setup: Frank and the therapist witness the gang drinking from cans
jokes.punchline: The gang launches into an extended testimonial about the advantages of canned wine — 'conducive to my violent hand gestures,' 'no spillage' — culminating in a live demonstration
jokes.explanation: The final major canned wine beat. Dennis's lecture about mobility and gesturing while accidently spilling a little mid-demonstration is a good self-undermining physical bit. The evangelism of Frank's idea to Frank completes the irony loop.

jokes.text: Dennis demonstrates canned wine hand-gesture superiority by almost spilling on the therapist while making his point
jokes.setup: Dennis is extolling the no-spill advantages of canned wine
jokes.punchline: While demonstrating that canned wine prevents spills, he nearly spills on the therapist — 'I spilled a little'
jokes.explanation: Good ironic visual gag — Dennis proving canned wine doesn't spill while spilling it. 'I spilled a little' as a sheepish admission undercuts his entire argument while he's still making it. Good self-undermining structure.

jokes.text: The therapist tries to regain control: 'People, I — I'm sorry, but how do you guys wanna proceed from here? Because I'm a little confused.' The gang: 'Ohh!'
jokes.setup: The intervention has completely devolved; the therapist tries to refocus
jokes.punchline: The gang's collective 'Ohh!' — as if she's said something embarrassing — followed by dismissing her contribution entirely
jokes.explanation: Good beat showing the gang's total unwillingness to engage with professional help. The therapist's confusion is the last gasp of sanity in the episode.

jokes.text: The gang decides they 'got what they needed out of the intervention' and therefore can't pay the therapist
jokes.setup: The therapist tries to figure out next steps
jokes.punchline: The gang concludes the intervention was successful on their own terms — therefore they owe nothing — 'we did all the work, didn't we?'
jokes.explanation: Classic gang logic — they define success as whatever they did, then use that definition to justify not paying. The 'we did all the work, didn't we?' is a solid piece of self-serving rationalization.

jokes.text: The gang offers the therapist a can of wine as payment; she scoffs; they kick her out
jokes.setup: They've refused to pay the therapist
jokes.punchline: Their offered substitute payment is canned wine; when she declines, she's ejected without ceremony
jokes.explanation: Good final use of the canned wine gag — it's simultaneously the gang's highest compliment and completely inappropriate as professional payment. 'Take that shoulder-padded jacket and get the hell out' is a good Dee button.

jokes.text: The gang gives each other high-fives: 'Great intervention! Great intervention work!' — celebrating a completely failed intervention
jokes.setup: The intervention accomplished nothing therapeutically and ended with salt-chasing, gun-waving, and therapist dismissal
jokes.punchline: The gang congratulates themselves enthusiastically on a job well done
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button. The gang's self-congratulation for a spectacular failure is a classic Sunny ending — they never learn, never grow, and always declare victory. The high-fives seal it as a parody of genuine intervention success stories.

tmdb_overview: Frank's behavior is more bizarre than usual---so bizarre that even the gang notice---so they decide to stage an intervention.
